thread.title: What El Niño's rapid return means for hurricane season
thread.title_full: What El Niño's rapid return means for hurricane season

author: Newsweek
title: What El Niño's rapid return means for hurricane season
text:
'The stronger the El Niño gets, the fewer named storms we're likely to get,' said AccuWeather hurricane expert Alex DaSilva.
AccuWeather has trimmed its forecast for the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season, citing the earlier-than-expected arrival of El Niño and increasing confidence that the climate pattern could strengthen significantly in the months ahead.of 11 to 16.
The revision comes after El Niño conditions emerged in June and as forecasters assess a growing likelihood that the phenomenonAccording to AccuWeather lead hurricane expert Alex DaSilva, El Niño has been the primary reason forecasters anticipated a quieter-than-average season from the outset.
"The stronger the El Niño gets, the fewer named storms we're likely to get," DaSilva said in a press release, noting that the 2015 Atlantic season, which coincided with a strong El Niño event, produced 11 named storms. “I think that is the sweet spot again this year. "While the projected number of named storms has been lowered, AccuWeather has not changed several other key elements of its seasonal outlook.
The company continues to forecast four to seven hurricanes, including two to four major hurricanes, and expects three to five storms to make direct impacts in the U.S. Forecasters at the outlet also say the areas facing the greatest risk remain the northern and eastern Gulf Coast, the southeastern U.S. coastline and parts of the Caribbean. DaSilva said storms that develop close to the coast can present a very different challenge than hurricanes that travel across the Atlantic after forming off Africa.
In those cases, warning times may be significantly shorter. AccuWeather said the lower storm forecast reflects El Niño's arrival in June and the increasing likelihood that the phenomenon will intensify, potentially reaching Super El Niño status later this year. The company estimates there is a 70 percent chance that a Super El Niño will emerge later in hurricane season and persist into early 2027. El Niño typically suppresses Atlantic hurricane activity by increasing wind shear across the basin, AccuWeather explained.
Strong wind shear disrupts the structure of developing tropical systems, making it more difficult for them to organize and intensify into named storms and hurricanes. In addition to forecasting fewer storms overall, AccuWeather said broader weather patterns during the summer and fall should reduce the risk of major tropical impacts along the central and lower Texas coastline. El Niño is the warm phase of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation, or ENSO, a natural climate pattern in the Pacific.
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration describes ENSO as involving shifts between warm and cool waters in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific that alter where ocean heat is released into the atmosphere, influencing circulation, temperatures, precipitation and other weather events.on average every two to seven years and typically lasts nine to 12 months. El Niño is the opposite of La Niña, the cool phase of ENSO, while neutral conditions fall between the two.
For El Niño conditions to form, sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific need to warm at least 0.5 degrees Celsius above normal and the atmosphere must also respond, including through weakened trade winds and a change in tropical rainfall patterns, NOAA says.
